messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 42

# Samuel's Careful Distance

Samuel moves through the warehouse with methodical precision, his seventy-nine-year-old body still capable of the work he's done for the past thirty-two years. He knows every aisle, every corner, every shadow. He prefers the night shift—fewer people, quieter, more predictable. His supervisor long ago stopped asking why he requested the graveyard hours. Samuel simply shows up, checks the inventory, restocks the shelves, and leaves. No complications.

But predictability is something Samuel has spent a lifetime chasing, ever since he was six years old and his mother's screams would pull him from sleep. He remembers the sounds more vividly than the images—his father's voice, low and dangerous; his mother's pleas; the crash of something breaking. Samuel would hide under his bed, hands over his ears, waiting for silence. His younger sister would crawl in beside him, trembling. He learned early that he couldn't stop what was happening in the next room, but he could be still enough, quiet enough, to keep his sister safe.

The violence stopped when Samuel was twelve. His father left one morning and never came back. Samuel felt relief and something else he couldn't name—a kind of hollowness that never quite filled.

Now, at seventy-nine, Samuel lives alone in a small apartment. He has a routine: work, home, sleep. He doesn't maintain close friendships, though people generally like him. He's reliable, quiet, competent. What they don't see is the way his body tenses when someone raises their voice, even in jest. What they don't notice is how he positions himself in rooms—always near an exit, always aware of where others are standing.

His marriage to Patricia ended twenty-three years ago. Samuel knows now that he was a difficult husband—withdrawn, hypervigilant, unable to be truly present. When Patricia would raise her voice during arguments, Samuel would shut down completely, sometimes leaving the house for hours. She wanted closeness; he could only offer distance. He couldn't explain to her that her anger, even reasonable anger, transported him somewhere else entirely. She eventually stopped trying.

Since Patricia left, Samuel has had no romantic relationships. The thought of living with someone again creates a low-level anxiety that sits in his chest like a stone. What if he couldn't protect them? What if he became like his father? What if he failed in some fundamental way?

At night, particularly on his nights off, Samuel sometimes lies awake replaying fragments of memories—not always his own. He finds himself imagining his mother's fear, his sister's confusion. He wonders what became of his father, whether the man ever felt remorse. These thoughts come unbidden, unwelcome, and they keep him awake until dawn.

He's noticed lately that his hands shake more than they used to, especially in the mornings. He startles easily when coworkers approach from behind. Last month, someone dropped a box near him, and Samuel found himself on the ground, heart racing, unable to explain to the concerned young worker why he'd reacted so violently.

Samuel doesn't talk about any of this. He comes to work, does his job, goes home. He's survived this long by being careful, by maintaining control, by keeping people at arm's length. It's a lonely way to live, but it's the way he knows.
